title: When it comes to systemic change, could dialogue be your best servant?
author: John Hill
source: Clear Leaders, shared via Zora Artis (zoraartis.substack.com), August 26, 2026
summary: Leadership and systemic team coach John Hill, sharing his essay through colleague Zora Artis's newsletter, argues that senior leadership teams mistake reporting and discussion for genuine dialogue, and that the distinction matters enormously for organizational alignment. Drawing on physicist and dialogue theorist David Bohm, he contrasts discussion (which "means to break things up" and rewards the most persuasive voice regardless of correctness) with dialogue, which requires suspending one's own convictions long enough to actually listen to and explore someone else's view. Hill identifies four levels at which dialogue delivers value: personally, by developing sustained attention; interpersonally, by building patience and genuine inquiry; at team level, by surfacing misalignment discussion tends to bury; and at system level, by widening what he calls system awareness. He connects this directly to the global employee-engagement crisis, currently around 20 percent actively engaged per Gallup's 2026 report, arguing that decisions cascaded top-down without genuine dialogue inevitably produce less commitment the further people are from where the decision was made.
points: Distinguishes discussion from dialogue using David Bohm's framing: discussion 'means to break things up' and rewards the most persuasive voice, while dialogue requires suspending one's own convictions to genuinely explore someone else's view.

Identifies four distinct levels at which dialogue delivers value: personal (developing sustained attention), interpersonal (adult behaviors like patience and inquiry), team (surfacing misalignment discussion buries), and system (widening system awareness).
Cites Nancy Kline's research finding that how well people think for themselves depends heavily on how they are being treated by the people around them in the moment.

Links weak dialogue practice directly to the global employee-engagement crisis (Gallup's 2026 report shows roughly 20% actively engaged, down from 23% in 2022), arguing top-down cascaded decisions inevitably produce less commitment the further people are from the decision.
quotes: Discussion really means to break things up. In a dialogue there is no attempt to gain points, or to make your particular view prevail.
If everyone has a different opinion, it will merely be a struggle of opinions, and the one who is strongest will win. It may not necessarily be the right one. It may be that none of them are right.
Dialogue asks something different: that you suspend your own convictions long enough to properly listen to, understand and explore someone else's.

The most important factor in whether or not people could think for themselves, afresh, at a given moment seemed to be how they were being treated by the people with them. How well we're attended to shapes how well we think.

In some ways, dialogue is quite easy to learn but difficult to do. Turn taking, listening with real attention, enquiry, appreciation, none of it is complicated in itself. What's hard is the discipline of it: staying with it when the pull to persuade, defend, or interrupt is strong.
